articles.author: Charlotte Jansen
articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. Continue reading...

articles.description: From the first lady’s Amazon documentary to Barron’s energy drink, the family is raking it in during Donald’s second term. For the non-refundable price of $150 (£115) you get one black-and-white digital image of the first lady sitting on a chair and one photo in which she is posing next to a clapperboard. According to Melania’s website, she and “Ms von Unwerth worked collaboratively during a two-day shoot to develop this visual narrative”. Continue reading...

articles.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures
articles.description: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Stream Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
articles.description: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London? Continue reading...

articles.description: By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left). Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth. Continue reading...

articles.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
articles.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA IV’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.author: Leslie Felperin
articles.title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
articles.description: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.title: Cookie fever! How does Marks & Spencer knock out so many viral food sensations?
articles.description: Chicken kievs, ‘picky bits’, strawberry and cream sandwiches: the hits have been coming for almost half a century. Now Kathryn Turner, M&S’s head of product development, has become a social media celebrity. What’s the secret ingredient? The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer , after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster . How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits? You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatever the flavour, there is always chocolate in them, and always more of it than you’d credit. Even the packaging on the M&S cookies – clear, crinkly – has the main-event feel of a bouquet or a hamper. Except if you put these cookies in a box, that box would be ginormous, and people would say: “I can’t eat five of those – don’t be stupid.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery
articles.description: Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke. articles.title: ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?
articles.description: Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling. From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football. articles.description: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. articles.author: Fergal Kinney
articles.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
articles.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.description: These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Bill McGuire
articles.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis? | Bill McGuire
articles.description: Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like It’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature mark could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region. We continue to pump out the CO 2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year , with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Continue reading...

articles.title: Soaring popularity of pickleball linked to eye injuries and disease, doctors warn
articles.description: Woman hit in eye developed glaucoma as a result, with other injuries including retinal tears Doctors have issued a warning about eye injuries linked to the rapid rise in popularity of pickleball, after a woman in her early 50s who was hit in the eye during a game developed glaucoma. After emergency treatment, she was discharged from hospital and her symptoms seemed to be resolving. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tim Dowling
articles.title: ‘Two million people tuned in to see me mash potatoes!’ Gregor Fisher on his remarkable rebirth after Rab C Nesbitt
articles.description: For almost 30 years Fisher played a drunk in a string vest. Now a new generation has come to know him through his cooking videos. He talks about family secrets, cancelled shows and the correct approach to butter Gregor Fisher’s kitchen is so tidy – it looks as if he has just finished cleaning it – that I begin to worry he has forgotten (or was possibly never apprised of) our arrangement. After he makes me a coffee and we sit at the square table, I feel obliged to raise the subject: aren’t we gonna cook something? “I thought we’d do some brunch,” he says. He steps into his larder and returns a moment later with the makings of kedgeree, prepared and covered in clingfilm: chopped onions, minced shallots, hard-boiled eggs, halibut from a fishmonger in Largs. articles.author: Interview by Liam Pape
articles.title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
articles.description: The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May Continue reading...

articles.author: Nathalie Tocci
articles.title: Europe’s big threat is not Trump and Putin redrawing the map. It’s our own learned helplessness | Natalie Tocci
articles.description: The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0 The first ever trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was rich in symbolism and empty of substance. Many Europeans, filled with anxiety about the Chinese, Russian and US presidents potentially colluding, saw chilling echoes of the Yalta conference in 1945, when Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt redrew the map of Europe. But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. Far more meaningful last week than Shenzhen was a gathering in Berlin , held at exactly the same time. Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Macfarlane says trust in Cop to deliver change on climate is ‘misplaced’

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.title: A timeline of Jensen Huang’s affair scandal, from quitting Nvidia to his return
articles.description: CEO behind Nvidia’s meteoric rise stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then was reinstated days later Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. The announcement of his resignation came on 12 November. A week and a half later, he was reinstated as the chief executive in a unanimous vote by Nvidia’s board. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.
